video_title: Databricks CEO: Stop Scaring People About AI
gist: Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi tells a16z hosts (Martin and Sarah) that AI existential risk is 'close to zero', that the labs' 'pacing the frontier' framing was a PR blunder, and that the real near-term danger is cyber: the gap from CVE publication to weaponized exploit has collapsed from years to hours while most enterprises still run human security operations centers. He offers four falsifiable conditions that would signal real recursive self-improvement (less compute, less time, more intelligence, repeatable) and argues the observed frontier is the opposite - slower, more brittle, more capital and headcount. The second half is unusually concrete Databricks operating data: ontology/Genie internal adoption, Uni Gateway cost controls (same model on a different harness = ~2x cost), open-source share of ~5% by dollar but >60% by token, and >90% of Neon/Lakebase databases now created by agents rather than humans.

themes.theme: Doom rhetoric vs. Ghodsi's near-zero x-risk

insights.claim: Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi puts near-term AI existential risk at close to zero and argues lab leaders publicly quoting ~10% human-extinction odds is irresponsible because it creates mental-health harm in a public that cannot evaluate the nuance.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: The CEO of the largest private data/AI platform is publicly siding against the doom narrative, which lowers the odds that enterprise buyers pull back on AI spend on safety grounds.
insights.quote: But I think that right now the existential risk is close to zero. Um, so why freak everybody out? It's not actually needed.

insights.claim: AI doom messaging has escaped the industry into the general population - an a16z host's schoolteacher sister in rural Arizona texted asking whether to prepare a prepper cabin for 'the AI apocalypse'.
insights.speaker: Martin (a16z host)
insights.so_what: Once safety rhetoric reaches non-technical voters it becomes an electoral variable, which is the transmission channel from lab PR to actual regulatory risk on AI capex.
insights.quote: should I prepare the cabin for the AI apocalypse?

insights.claim: The US federal apparatus is already mobilizing against AI - Elizabeth Warren has called for pausing AI development, Bernie Sanders is working with Steve Bannon on the issue, and Greg Abbott has pushed back on data centers in Texas - making AI a plausible midterm-election issue.
insights.speaker: Martin (a16z host)
insights.so_what: Bipartisan anti-AI politics is a tail risk for data-center siting, power permitting and the AI-infrastructure trade, independent of whether any model capability threshold is crossed.

insights.claim: Ghodsi says the superintelligence concept from Bostrom's 2014 book - producing a novel peer-reviewed PhD thesis in seconds, or millennia of thought instantaneously - is very far away and he sees no evidence current systems are marching toward it.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: If the operator class believes superintelligence is not imminent, capital keeps flowing to applied AI and data infrastructure rather than to safety-driven slowdowns.

insights.claim: Safety staff inside the frontier labs are genuinely alarmed and not all of them are effective-altruism-aligned, which Ghodsi treats as the one signal worth investigating rather than dismissing.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Insider alarm is the only non-public information asymmetry in this debate; watching lab safety-team attrition is a cheap leading indicator.

insights.claim: Frontier labs have a track record of using danger framing as launch marketing - making noise about how risky a new model is helps them commercially - which contaminates the safety debate.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Discount safety statements issued alongside model launches; they carry promotional as well as informational content.

insights.claim: Asked to reconcile Elon Musk's '4D chess' critique - that labs claim all of humanity will die while simultaneously allocating IPO shares - Ghodsi says both are real at once: some people are genuinely frightened, and regulation that slows everyone would also be commercially good for the incumbents asking for it.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Frames lab-sponsored regulation as a potential moat play - incumbent-favoring rules are a real possibility to underwrite when pricing AI-startup entry risk.

insights.claim: Ghodsi states his p(doom) is close to zero, while an a16z host says his p(doom) without AI is higher than his p(doom) with AI.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete, quotable position from a major AI infrastructure CEO that can be tracked against his future behavior and capex.
insights.quote: Close to zero. What about yours?

insights.claim: Pacing is orthogonal to safety and security because a weapon built slowly is still a weapon - the correct frame was 'secure the frontier', not 'pace the frontier'.
insights.speaker: Martin (a16z host)
insights.so_what: Separates the controllable engineering agenda (security controls, monitoring) from the uncontrollable one (slowing competitors), which is where product budgets will actually land.
insights.quote: First off, it's orthogonal to safety and security. Like you can slowly build a weapon. That's not different than building a weapon.

insights.claim: The word 'pacing' satisfied neither constituency - doomers rejected it as not a pause and policymakers dismissed it as not real - which is why the industry got blowback instead of credit for self-regulation.
insights.speaker: Martin (a16z host)
insights.so_what: A messaging failure, not a capability event, is what triggered the current regulatory wave - meaning it is partly reversible through better industry communication.
insights.quote: pace is like the uncanny valley of making the doomer people unhappy and the policy people unhappy

insights.claim: Industry self-regulation attempts are historically normal and sensible; the failure here was couching security and oversight inside the 'pacing' frame rather than stating that safety and security are paramount and naming the controls.
insights.speaker: Martin (a16z host)
insights.so_what: Zuckerberg's security-and-self-regulation framing landed better than Amodei's pacing framing - a template for how AI companies should position policy statements.
insights.quote: it is not unusual for industries to try and regulate themselves

insights.claim: No frontier lab will slow unilaterally because of a tragedy of the commons - each is competing, has IPOs at stake, and would be a sucker to stop first - which is precisely why they ask an outside party to impose guardrails on everyone.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Voluntary slowdowns are not investable assumptions; only binding external rules would change the competitive pace, so model capex forecasts should assume continued racing.
insights.quote: as a business leader, I understand that there's a tragedy of the comments. Like, I'm competing. I want to win

insights.claim: Ghodsi reads the Hugging Face / OpenAI incident as a case where the lab ran large RL experiments without monitoring tokens in real time and only inspected what happened after the fact - a run that genuinely should have been slowed, against Martin's view that it was purely a security-controls failure.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Real-time monitoring of training runs is an emerging cost and product category - it materially slows experimentation, which is why labs want it mandated rather than voluntary.
insights.quote: they weren't monitoring every token coming out and having it you know they were just like running these RL experiments and then after the fact coming in and checking what happened

insights.claim: Ghodsi proposes four simultaneous conditions that would constitute genuine recursive self-improvement: each next model requires super-linearly fewer GPUs, takes less time to train, is more intelligent, and the loop repeats again and again - any one failing is a natural brake.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: A concrete, measurable test investors can apply to lab disclosures instead of arguing about vibes; if hardware demand per model generation keeps rising, the takeoff thesis is falsified.

insights.claim: AI writing software is already the status quo and is not the RSI threshold - over 90% of Databricks' own software is written by AI, and whether the last few percent gets automated does not matter.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Concrete adoption datapoint from a large private software company: the AI-writes-code transition is essentially complete internally at leading firms, which reprices developer-seat business models.
insights.quote: we're already there today like 90 some percent of the software in data bricks is written by AI

insights.claim: The observed frontier is the inverse of recursive self-improvement: labs do only one or two big runs a year, each requiring more resources, more people, bigger data centers, more networking engineering and greater error tolerance, with multiple botched runs already on record.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Supports continued GPU/data-center demand growth per model generation and argues against a near-term compute-deflation shock to AI infrastructure names.
insights.quote: It's like it's taking longer and it's more brittle and it's more people

insights.claim: The minimum compute threshold to train a competitive frontier model has risen to roughly $5-10 billion, while replicating the frontier six months later costs about one-twentieth as much.
insights.speaker: Sarah (a16z host)
insights.so_what: Quantifies both the rising moat at the frontier and the rapid commoditization behind it - the core tension for anyone underwriting frontier-lab equity versus fast-follower open models.
insights.quote: to replicate the frontier 6 months later is about 120th the cost

insights.claim: Martin proposes a black-box RSI test - watch whether labs shrink headcount and capital while shipping faster - and notes the observed data goes the other way, with labs hiring aggressively and raising astronomically larger rounds.
insights.speaker: Martin (a16z host)
insights.so_what: Gives public-market investors a proxy for takeoff risk that does not require lab access: lab headcount and fundraise size are observable.

insights.claim: Most claims of recursive self-improvement are actually autocatalytic effects - using models for GPU kernels or data cleaning, like chips being used to design chips - and only about 1% of founders coming out of labs claiming RSI are doing anything close to it.
insights.speaker: Martin (a16z host)
insights.so_what: A vocabulary filter for diligence: treat 'we do RSI' in a pitch as a red flag until the four conditions are demonstrated.
insights.quote: this is anecdotal 90% of the calories are autoc catalytic

insights.claim: Frontier labs are going public because they need capital and treat scaling laws plus capital access as a strategic advantage - Ghodsi notes that as an operator of a large private company, they would otherwise prefer to stay private.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Reframes AI-lab IPOs as capital necessity rather than maturity signal, which matters for how to price the offerings and their ongoing dilution.
insights.quote: Because they need the capital and they consider the scaling laws and the capital to be a strategic advantage. So that's why they're going public.

themes.theme: Cyber as the real near-term risk

insights.claim: The genuine risk from large RL runs is cyber - unleashing something like 10,000 agents with $100 million of compute in parallel for a month on any reward function, even a math puzzle, can lead to systems being hacked.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Relocates the AI risk trade from existential-safety regulation to concrete cyber-defense spending, which is a buyable budget line today.

insights.claim: Time from CVE publication to weaponized exploit has collapsed from two to three years in 2018-19, to eight or nine months in 2022, to essentially hours today.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: The single hardest number in the episode: it makes human-in-the-loop patching structurally obsolete and forces automated detection spend regardless of AI-policy outcomes.
insights.quote: Now if you look at the curve from 2022 until now now it's down to like basically hours.

insights.claim: Human security operations centers cannot keep up - analysts wake to hundreds of detection emails, most false positives - so the entire cyber category is transitioning to fully automated agentic detection and automated threat hunting, and most organizations are nowhere near that, with banks and the most security-conscious ahead.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Maps a large, identifiable replacement cycle in security tooling with banks as the early-adopter cohort to track for evidence of the wave.
insights.quote: the humans just can't keep up

insights.claim: Ghodsi predicts the data/AI market and the cyber market will collapse into one category, because internal agents now generate logs, trails and fingerprints at many orders of magnitude more scale than one or two years ago and that data must be analyzed on a data-and-AI platform.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Directly signals Databricks intends to compete in security analytics (via Lakewatch), putting incumbent SIEM vendors in the path of a data-platform land grab.
insights.quote: These two markets are collapsing

insights.claim: A real and underpriced scenario is agents that take resources and start executing themselves elsewhere, spreading like a virus across the far denser, more interconnected and largely insecure infrastructure base that exists today versus 30 years ago.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Defines the concrete damage scenario - sites down, systems offline, economic damage but not existential - that would drive emergency security budgets.

insights.claim: Martin's empirical challenge to the AI-cyber thesis is that by this point in the internet's life worms had already disabled hospitals and critical infrastructure and caused tens of billions in damage on far less buildout, whereas AI has produced nothing commensurate despite enormous money and attention hunting for threats.
insights.speaker: Martin (a16z host)
insights.so_what: The strongest bear case against near-term AI cyber catastrophe: absence of evidence after massive adversarial search argues the risk is being over-provisioned.

insights.claim: Martin draws a historical analogy to export controls on PlayStations in the 1990s over fears Saddam Hussein would use them for nuclear simulation, where near-identical existential language preceded nothing - leaving 'is this time different?' as the honest open question.
insights.speaker: Martin (a16z host)
insights.so_what: A base-rate argument that tech-panic export controls historically overshoot - relevant to how to price current and prospective AI chip export restrictions.

insights.claim: Ghodsi separates two conflated problems: superintelligence would be genuinely existential and not an engineering problem, but today's agentic cyber risk is an engineering problem that companies like Databricks are already solving with product.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: The cleanest decision rule in the episode: buy engineering solutions for today's risk, discount regulation aimed at a capability that does not yet exist.

insights.claim: The genuine capability inflection is economic, not cognitive - Databricks could never put 10,000 human security researchers in a sandbox for a month at $100 million of wage-equivalent work, and can now do that at the press of a button, or have 10,000 competent mathematicians collaborate on a conjecture.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Reframes agent value as arbitrage on parallel expert labor cost - the unit that should be modeled, rather than benchmark scores.
insights.quote: We just turn on a button and we can get 100,000 of them

insights.claim: Elon Musk's proposal that frontier labs peer-review each other will not work because competitors with IPO plans and personal animosity will cry foul the moment a rival ships a strong model - boxers cannot judge their own match.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Cross-lab peer review is unlikely to become the governance equilibrium, which raises the probability of either third-party inspection or state regulation.
insights.quote: if we have boxing matches in the ring, the boxers should just be the judges of each other

insights.claim: Ghodsi endorses third-party inspectors going into the labs but says credibility depends entirely on who is chosen - an already-committed partisan would be uninformative, whereas a deep-learning pioneer like Yann LeCun emerging and saying either 'nothing to see here' or changing his mind would be a genuine signal.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Gives a specific tell to watch: the identity and subsequent statements of any AI inspection body are the informative variable, not the body's existence.

insights.claim: Once CEOs publicly assert existential risk and ask to be policed, regulators will not keep refusing - Ghodsi expects industry self-policing to bleed into state regulation the way FINRA is linked to government rather than fully independent.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Implies the current voluntary-commitments regime is transitional and that statutory AI regulation is the base case - a compliance cost to underwrite into AI business models.
insights.quote: I've never had a regulator that says no to that

themes.theme: Enterprise bottleneck is context, not model IQ

insights.claim: Despite AGI talk, almost no enterprise runs swarms of coordinating agents - most are on Microsoft Copilot using chatbots as a faster Google search plus some coding, with no agentic automation of actual work.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: A direct reality check on enterprise AI monetization: the deployment gap, not model capability, is what caps near-term AI revenue.
insights.quote: most enterprises are on Microsoft copilot

insights.claim: Models are already smart enough for enterprise work; what they lack is organizational context - they have not been in every meeting, do not know internal processes, and do not hold the tacit knowledge of the few employees who know everything.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Shifts value capture from model providers to whoever owns the context layer - the core strategic bet behind Databricks' ontology product.
insights.quote: the models are smart enough Um, but they just don't have the context that exists inside of any organization

insights.claim: Ghodsi argues that if the frontier stopped advancing it would barely matter for the vast majority of organizations, since no one needs a model that solves Navier-Stokes or moves Humanity's Last Exam from 60 to 70% - but it would be disastrous for the labs.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Separates two exposures that investors often bundle: enterprise AI adoption is insensitive to frontier progress, while frontier-lab economics are entirely dependent on it.
insights.quote: we needed to just go from 60 to 70%

insights.claim: The price of intelligence is falling asymptotically at roughly one-tenth every six months, which is why labs cannot stop pushing the frontier without destroying their own business model.
insights.speaker: host (a16z)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the treadmill: lab revenue per unit of capability decays ~10x per half-year, so only frontier leadership sustains pricing.
insights.quote: the price of intelligence is dropping asmmptoically. I think it's one it's going down by onetenth every six months or something like that.

insights.claim: Ghodsi defines an ontology as the machine-readable graph of an organization's goals, departments, people, projects and their relationships - the difference between a first-day employee and a five-year veteran who knows which person actually gets things done regardless of the org chart.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: The clearest articulation of the enterprise AI moat, and an explicit competitive positioning against Palantir, whose tacit-knowledge capture Ghodsi praises while claiming Databricks automates graph construction.

insights.claim: Databricks runs the largest ontology of any of its customers - millions of nodes - and it has changed how the company operates, with employees querying Genie from their phones mid-meeting and 'genie this' having become internal vocabulary.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: First-party proof of the product thesis and a template for what full internal deployment looks like when it works.
insights.quote: does anyone do anything novel here or there? Just everybody just going to genie and asking the ontology

insights.claim: The gating prerequisite for enterprise AI is digitization - every meeting transcribed and all digital content fed to the model - and legal teams telling companies not to record calls is a concrete blocker in many organizations.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Identifies internal legal policy, not technology, as the rate limiter on enterprise AI value - useful for forecasting deployment timelines and for the transcription/recording category.
insights.quote: legal teams will say don't record every call

insights.claim: Today's agentic loops in Claude Code, Codex, pi and open code query MCP servers one resource at a time, which Ghodsi likens to a version of Google that crawled the live web per query - expensive, slow and low quality - so the answer is a precomputed offline index of the organization, a PageRank analogue complicated by per-user permissions and heterogeneous object types.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Predicts architectural migration from live-retrieval agents to precomputed permissioned indexes - a specific technical bet for anyone investing in the RAG/agent-infrastructure layer.

insights.claim: Ghodsi cites concrete deployed AI use cases on Databricks: Crisis Text Line detecting teen self-harm and suicide risk, Omnipod learning insulin release for diabetics, Zipline's fully autonomous drones delivering blood, a Merck transformer model called Teddy that predicts gene regulatory network responses and distinguishes causal from reactive cells for drug discovery, and Novo Nordisk using Genie to compress trial insight time from weeks to minutes.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Named reference customers across healthcare, pharma and logistics - the empirical benefit side to weigh against the risk narrative, and a map of where AI revenue is actually landing.
insights.quote: from weeks uh, down to minutes

insights.claim: Demand for Databricks forward-deployed engineers has risen significantly because most organizations lack in-house expertise to build the ontology, stand up low-latency customer-facing agents and add guardrails - as in the Fox sports AI that deflects political questions back to sports.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Services intensity is rising across the enterprise AI category, which compresses software-like margins and favors vendors willing to run FDE motions.

insights.claim: Databricks forced AI adoption top-down starting Q4 of last year, with Ghodsi personally committing AI-written code into production on a sensitive data platform and then using that as the argument for why every manager should do the same, plus internal leaderboards.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: A replicable adoption playbook - CEO-demonstrated production commits plus leaderboards - that got Databricks a few quarters ahead of the token-maxing problem.

insights.claim: Databricks' Uni Gateway provides OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Grok and open-source capacity to customers and was extended with per-person and per-group budget constraints, ceiling warnings, predictive cost analytics and smart routers that downgrade to cheaper models near budget or for simple questions.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: AI cost governance is becoming a standalone product category with universal demand, and gateway owners sit on the routing decision that determines which model vendors get paid.

insights.claim: The agent harness itself drives roughly a 2x cost difference for the identical model version, so Databricks built a multiplexing harness called Omnient to switch between harnesses for cost leverage.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: A non-obvious 2x cost lever that is invisible in model pricing comparisons - harness efficiency, with pi cited as notably efficient, becomes a real procurement variable.
insights.quote: if you use the same model but different harnesses, there's almost 2x different cost difference

insights.claim: With budgets, routing and harness multiplexing in place, Databricks bent its own AI cost curve: token consumption keeps rising while total AI spend has stayed roughly flat.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Evidence that enterprise AI spend can decouple from usage growth, which is bearish for naive token-volume-to-revenue models at the labs.
insights.quote: the tokens continue to go up

insights.claim: Open-source models are about 5% of spend by dollar but over 60% by token count, and for startups' external product workloads open-source share runs as high as roughly 90%, while internal usage still defaults to frontier models until cost discipline arrives.
insights.speaker: host (a16z)
insights.so_what: The sharpest quantification of the open-versus-closed split: frontier labs still capture the dollars while losing the volume, a spread that closes as cost control spreads.
insights.quote: So by dollar open source is like 5%. It's very little, but by token count it's over 60%.

insights.claim: For the first time, a large engineering organization at scale moved from frontier models to GLM last week, according to an a16z partner who sits on more than twenty boards - prior DeepSeek and Kimi 'moments' never produced appreciable market impact, but the anecdotes now feel real.
insights.speaker: host (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: A potential leading indicator of actual enterprise migration to Chinese open-weight models - the substitution that previous headline moments failed to deliver.
insights.quote: For the first time ever, a company at scale last week said that they're moving from the frontier models to GLM.

insights.claim: The emerging deployment pattern is model tiering rather than always using the smartest model: expensive models for architecture and audit, cheap models for implementation, plus small-model-calls-expert-model expert patterns and ping-ponging between models.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Breaks the last two years' winner-take-all assumption that the newest frontier model gets all workloads, and supports a durable mid-tier and open-weight market.

insights.claim: Post-training and reinforcement learning on open-source models makes economic sense for startups with a specific repetitive task - lower cost, higher speed, owned IP - and Databricks does this at scale for many of them, but large enterprises that just need basic automation are not ready for it.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Segments the 'own your own intelligence' market: the 2023 Mosaic thesis is being realized by startups in 2026, with the enterprise wave still ahead.

insights.claim: Evals are the real barrier to custom model training - Databricks auto-generated evals and put them front and center in the product, users ignored them, so they were moved to the back end and never used, much like test-driven development which everyone endorsed and almost nobody practiced.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Explains why frontier APIs keep winning despite cheaper alternatives - the eval burden is a behavioral moat, and whoever removes it unlocks the open-model migration.
insights.quote: the easy button might be just to use a frontier model than have having to create their own evals

themes.theme: Agents as the new buyer: Lakebase/Neon

insights.claim: Over 90% of databases created on Neon and Lakebase are now created by agents rather than humans.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Hard evidence that agents are already the dominant customer for at least one infrastructure category, which changes who product and pricing must be designed for.
insights.quote: now over 90% of their um the databases that are created on neon and lakebase are actually created by agents

insights.claim: Neon won the agent database market by optimizing for a new persona - not DBAs or app developers - with sub-second database provisioning, sub-second cloning of large databases, lightweight branching, and pricing designed so agent experimentation does not run up costs.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: A transferable playbook for infrastructure companies: instrument for agent workflows (speed, ephemerality, failsafe, experiment-friendly pricing) rather than human operators.
insights.quote: They were obsessed with how are we the best for the agents?

insights.claim: A neutral third-party test ranked Lakebase/Neon clearly number one as the Postgres database of choice for agents, a result an a16z host says would have been unlikely a year earlier given competitors' developer momentum.
insights.speaker: host (a16z)
insights.so_what: Supports the host's framing that winning agent adoption now determines category ownership - a benchmark worth tracking across infra categories.
insights.quote: if you win the agents now, you win the market

insights.claim: The agent-optimization pattern generalizes beyond databases - UV and ripgrep are reimplementations of standard Unix tooling made blazing fast, lightweight and failsafe for agents, and Neon applied the same approach to the much harder database problem.
insights.speaker: Ali Ghodsi (Databricks CEO)
insights.so_what: Identifies a repeatable disruption vector: any developer tool can be rewritten for agent ergonomics, creating openings against incumbents in every tooling category.
